Previous imaging obtained a year prior showed hepatomegaly (18 cm) and mild perinephric stranding bilaterally. On admission, physical examination findings revealed tense ascites without telangiectasia, jaundice, or other skin changes. Initial workup showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 11.8 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 106 μm3), thrombocytopenia (88 × 103/μL), normal white blood cell count (5.19 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]) with lymphopenia (0.72 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), hypoalbuminemia (2.2 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]), elevated alkaline phosphatase (655 U/L; reference, 41-133 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]), and hyperbilirubinemia (total, 2.1 mg/dL; reference, 0.3-1.2; direct, 1.3 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104]) with otherwise normal levels of creatinine, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Findings of activated partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio were also normal, and there was no significant proteinuria. An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). Several abdominopelvic FDG avid lymph nodes were also seen. Perinephric fibrosis and hepatomegaly were significantly worse compared with previous imaging obtained 12 months prior.

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

{

}

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"

  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

On admission, physical examination findings revealed tense ascites without telangiectasia, jaundice, or other skin changes. Findings of activated partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio were also normal, and there was no significant proteinuria. An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). Several abdominopelvic FDG avid lymph nodes were also seen. Perinephric fibrosis and hepatomegaly were significantly worse compared with previous imaging obtained 12 months prior.

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

You MUST pick a stage from this list.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.caption: A,18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) showing FDG uptake in the perirenal space (white arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions with FDG uptake (yellow arrowheads). case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.
